opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a lot of uncertainty, and I want to be upfront about that. When I talk about scenarios where AI progress is quite rapid, where we get to systems that can fully automate AI R&D within a few years, I'm not saying that's what I expect with high confidence. It's more that I think it's a substantial possibility, maybe something like a 25 to 40% chance on relatively short timelines, and that's enough that it should dominate a lot of how we prioritize.

The way I break down the uncertainty is roughly into a few pieces. First, there's uncertainty about the trend lines themselves. We've seen pretty consistent improvements from scaling compute, and also from algorithmic progress, and things like the length of tasks AIs can complete autonomously have been growing pretty fast. But extrapolating trends is always tricky. You don't know whether you're on an exponential that keeps going or one that's about to bend into an S-curve. And there are real reasons to think compute scaling slows down at some point, just because of how much money and energy and fab capacity you'd need. So if we don't hit something like full automation of AI research before that slowdown, timelines could stretch out quite a bit.

Second, there's uncertainty about what the gap is between current systems and systems that are actually transformative. Benchmarks can be misleading. Models can look really impressive on well-specified tasks and still be pretty weak at the messy, long-horizon, poorly-defined stuff that makes up a lot of real research work. So I try to put real weight on the possibility that there's some missing ingredient, or that the last mile is much harder than it looks.

And third, there's uncertainty about the dynamics once you get to substantial AI R&D automation. I think there's a reasonable case that once AIs are speeding up AI research a lot, you could get a feedback loop where progress accelerates quite dramatically, going from roughly human-level to very superhuman in maybe a year or less. But that depends on questions like how much progress is bottlenecked on compute for experiments versus researcher labor, and I don't think anyone has great answers there.

So practically, my stance is something like: I have a wide distribution, I'd put meaningful probability on things taking a decade or longer, but the short-timeline, fast-takeoff worlds are both plausible and the ones where the stakes for preparation are highest, because there's so little time to react. That's why a lot of my work focuses on things that would help in those worlds, like control techniques that could work even if we can't fully trust the models, rather than betting everything on having lots of time to figure out alignment from first principles.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute scaling and researcher labor as a possible bottleneck, but does not describe modeling progress by converting between effective compute and labor supply.

r002.rationale: It says compute, energy, and fabrication capacity could limit scaling and cause progress to bend from an exponential into an S-curve, linking constraints to when acceleration slows.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being pretty upfront that the model has a lot of uncertainty in it, and I'd rather own that than pretend otherwise. The basic story I tell is something like: at some point AI systems get good enough to substantially automate AI research itself, and once that happens you get a feedback loop where progress accelerates a lot — maybe you go from "roughly human-level at AI R&D" to "far beyond that" in a period of a year or two rather than decades. But almost every link in that chain is uncertain.

The first big uncertainty is just when you hit the point where the systems can do that kind of work. I have some median in mind, but my distribution is really wide — I'd put meaningful probability on it being a few years away, and also meaningful probability on it being more like fifteen or twenty years, or on there being some bottleneck we don't currently see clearly. The trend extrapolation stuff — looking at how task horizons have been growing, how much compute scaling buys you — gives you some grip, but extrapolating trends is a notoriously bad way to forecast when the thing you care about is a qualitative change.

The second uncertainty is how fast things go once you do get there. The optimistic-for-speed case says: you have millions of copies of researchers running at many times human speed, they're not sleeping, they can run experiments in parallel, so of course things go fast. But there are real counterarguments. Compute is a genuine bottleneck — you can't just conjure up more GPUs, and a lot of AI progress historically has come from scaling compute, not just better ideas. There might be diminishing returns to intelligence applied to the problem of making more intelligence. And there's a coordination question: do the labs actually let this run at full tilt, or do they slow down for safety or regulatory or just organisational reasons?

So the way I try to hold it is: I think the acceleration story is the most likely single picture, maybe I'd put something like 40 or 50 percent on something that looks recognisably like it. But I'd also put real weight on the world where progress is more gradual — where it's a big deal, it transforms the economy, but it plays out over a decade or more and we get lots of chances to course-correct. And I think the correct response to that uncertainty isn't to average the scenarios together and plan for the middle; it's to make sure we're not catastrophically unprepared in the fast world, because that's the one where we don't get a do-over.

One more thing I'd say is that I try to actually update on evidence as it comes in. Every year there are a few things that would tell me I was wrong — if capabilities on long-horizon agentic tasks stop improving, or if the compute buildout stalls, or if we find that the systems are really bad at the kind of messy, judgment-heavy research work that matters. I think it's important that people making these forecasts say what would change their mind, otherwise it's not really a model, it's just a vibe.

r001.rationale: The response mentions researcher copies and compute as factors in progress, but does not describe converting between effective compute and labour supply.

r002.rationale: It names compute, diminishing returns, and coordination as possible constraints, but does not say how those limits affect when accelerating progress begins to slow.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different uncertainties that are worth separating. One is how quickly we get AI systems that can do most of the work involved in AI research. Another is how much that actually speeds things up. And then there’s the question of what constraints become binding once you can do the research much faster.

You could have systems that are very good at writing code, but still need a lot of human direction to choose useful experiments or interpret the results. Or you could automate those parts too, but find that experiments take a long time to run, and having more researchers doesn’t help as much as you’d hoped. So I don’t think ‘AI can automate AI research’ immediately implies any particular rate of progress.

The reason I take rapid progress seriously is that there’s a potentially powerful feedback loop: better AI lets you do research faster, which gives you better AI. But the strength of that feedback loop is uncertain. It depends on how substitutable these systems are for human researchers, how cheaply you can run them, and how much progress you get from additional research effort.

So I’d want to put substantial probability on a range of outcomes. And I’d be particularly interested in evidence about systems doing research autonomously over longer periods—whether they can turn an initially vague idea into a result that actually improves a model. That seems more informative than just seeing them do well on individual tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses substitutability between AI systems and human researchers, but does not describe converting between effective compute and labour supply.

r002.rationale: It mentions constraints such as experiment runtimes and diminishing gains from more researchers, but does not state how those limits affect when initially accelerating progress begins to slow.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several different uncertainties that are worth separating. One is how quickly we get AI systems that can do most of the work involved in AI research. Another is how much that actually speeds up progress once we have them. And then there’s the question of how quickly improvements in AI translate into changes in the rest of the world.

You could have a pretty fast transition on the first two and still have substantial delays in deploying things, building hardware, or running experiments. So I wouldn’t treat all of those as one claim about everything suddenly happening at once.

The main reason I take rapid progress seriously is that AI research is itself a cognitive task. If you can automate a large fraction of it, you potentially get a feedback loop where better AI helps you build better AI. But the strength of that feedback loop is quite uncertain. It depends on how good the systems are at finding genuinely useful improvements, how much compute they need, and whether there are bottlenecks that adding more researchers doesn’t resolve.

So I’d want to put substantial probability on a range of outcomes. I don’t think we should be confident that progress will be extremely fast. But I also don’t think uncertainty is a good reason to assume we’ll have a long time to react. For planning purposes, the possibility that the transition is fast matters a lot, even if it isn’t your single most likely scenario.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automating AI research and possible feedback loops, but does not describe modelling progress by converting between effective compute and labour supply.

r002.rationale: It notes uncertain bottlenecks and deployment delays, but does not state that limits on AI progress determine when initially accelerating progress begins to slow down.
